strengths: Originality: Jointly studying image resolution and sample size under random template deformations offers an interesting statistical perspective. The main originality lies in the resolution-dependent analysis and connection to CNN representation, building on established deformation and registration ideas.

Significance: The image-alignment procedure in Section 3.2 provides a simple, interpretable benchmark for exploiting known invariances. The constructive filter-bank argument in Appendix B also gives useful intuition for representing deformation-invariant classification with CNNs.

Presentation: The motivation, worked deformation examples, and illustrations make the framework accessible. Extensive proofs expose the reasoning behind the guarantees and facilitate technical scrutiny.

Limitations and ethics: The manuscript appropriately acknowledges computationally intractable optimization and discusses extensions involving noise, occlusion, and multiple templates. These acknowledgments are valuable. I identified no material ethical concerns in the theoretical work or MNIST experiments.
weaknesses: Soundness: Equation (27) does not define empirical misclassification error for labels in {0,1}. Its objective, -(1/n) sum_i k_i 1[q_2(X_i)>1/2], ignores false positives. A network always predicting class 1 is therefore a global minimizer for every training sample, yet its test error is 1-pi. This contradicts Theorem 4.1's vanishing bound as n increases. Equation (94) incorrectly equates this objective with ordinary 0-1 risk minimization. Although the intended objective appears repairable, the central learning guarantee is false for the estimator actually defined.

Soundness: The proof of Theorem 3.1 contains a substantive quantifier gap. Lemma A.3 establishes approximation to the normalized template for the existence of a suitable inverse B*. On page 29, this approximation is used for every pair of candidate inverses B_i and B. Since classifier (10) minimizes over all such pairs, controlling only suitable inverses does not exclude closer matches from the wrong class. A valid separation argument covering every searched transformation is needed.

Soundness of optimality claims: Theorem 3.7 constructs templates with identical pixel averages and ordinary L2 distance of order at least 1/d. It does not establish the corresponding lower bound for D in (12) or (21), which minimizes normalized distance over transformations and brightness. Consequently, the claimed matching optimality of the deformation-based separation condition does not follow from the presented lower bound.

Experimental evidence and significance: Section 5 fixes resolution at 28×28 and uses deformations of one or ten templates per class. It does not test the predicted dependence on resolution, separation, or deformation-class complexity. Moreover, the Adam-trained CNNs with local filters and pooling differ from the architecture and exact risk minimization analyzed theoretically. These experiments provide a limited qualitative illustration, rather than convincing validation of the central CNN guarantees.

Reproducibility: The supplied manuscript gives architectures and an Adam learning rate but omits the experimental training loss, epochs, batch sizes, deformation parameter ranges, and sufficient template-selection details. No code location is provided. Figure 8 reports medians over 30 repetitions without variability estimates. These omissions prevent reliable reproduction and assessment of the CNN comparison.

Presentation and mathematical consistency: Theorem 4.2, Lemma 4.3, and Proposition B.4 refer to the scaling-and-shifting separation quantity (21), whereas their general-deformation arguments use (12). These quantities are materially different; the statements and proofs must agree on which separation assumption supports the conclusions.
